title: What Stress Really Does to Your Brain
desc: Your heart pounds, your mouth goes dry, and your mind goes blank at exactly the wrong moment. In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined person, Jonah, through one stressful Monday and use it to explore what stress really does to your brain and body: where the word came from (Cannon and Selye), the alarm that fires in seconds, the slower wave of cortisol, why stress can sharpen or scramble your thinking, how it shapes memory, why a sense of control matters so much, what happens when the alarm never switches off, the surprising science of the stress mindset, why a hand to hold calms the brain, and gentle, research-based things that help. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. This video is for curiosity, not medical advice. The second half is a slow guided wind-down, so you can let the day go and drift off to sleep.
plan: b01: hook (Jonah, an imagined person, 7:42 on a Monday: train late, phone buzzing, heart pounding before a big talk at 9) + 'Tonight, we'll explore' list; stress is not the enemy, it is an ancient alarm; open loop: can believing something about stress change what it does to you (paid off b09)

b02: where the word comes from: Walter Cannon 1915 fight-or-flight, Cannon 1932 homeostasis (The Wisdom of the Body); Hans Selye 1936 Nature letter, rats and 'diverse nocuous agents', general adaptation syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion); Selye borrowed 'stress' from physics/engineering; Jonah on the platform

b03: the alarm in seconds: amygdala, hypothalamus, sympathetic nervous system, adrenaline from the adrenal glands (heart, breath, pupils, digestion paused); LeDoux 1996 The Emotional Brain, the quick 'low road' and slower 'high road' (snake vs stick); Jonah's pounding heart explained

b04: the slower wave: HPA axis and cortisol (peaks roughly 20-30 min after the stressor); daily rhythm and the cortisol awakening response (Pruessner et al. 1997, rises about 50-75% within 30 min of waking); Trier Social Stress Test (Kirschbaum, Pirke & Hellhammer 1993); Dickerson & Kemeny 2004 meta-analysis of 208 studies: social-evaluative threat + uncontrollability = biggest cortisol response; Jonah's 9:00 talk is exactly that

b05: stress and thinking: Yerkes & Dodson 1908 mice, the inverted U and Teigen 1994 caveat (over-generalised); Arnsten 2009 prefrontal cortex goes 'offline' under strong stress, older habits take over; Liston, McEwen & Casey 2009 PNAS medical students before exams (attention shifting worse, recovered after a month of lower stress); why Jonah forgets his first line

b06: stress and memory: Cahill, Prins, Weber & McGaugh 1994 Nature (propranolol removed the memory boost for the emotional story); flashbulb memories Brown & Kulik 1977 and Talarico & Rubin 2003 (confidence, not accuracy); Kuhlmann, Piel & Wolf 2005 stress hurts retrieval; Schwabe & Wolf 2009 stress pushes toward habits

b07: control: Glass & Singer 1972 noise and the button nobody pressed; Seligman & Maier 1967 learned helplessness and Maier & Seligman 2016 revision (passivity is the default, control is what is learned, prefrontal cortex); predictability; Jonah texts ahead to say he'll be late and feels calmer

b08: when the alarm never switches off: McEwen 1998 NEJM allostasis and allostatic load; Sapolsky 1994 Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers (zebras run then stop; we replay); Cohen, Tyrrell & Smith 1991 NEJM common cold (about 400 volunteers, more stress more colds); Kiecolt-Glaser et al. 1995 Lancet caregivers' wounds healed about nine days slower; careful, no clinical advice

b09: the stress mindset (pays off b01): Keller et al. 2012 Health Psychology (about 29,000 adults; high stress plus believing it harms health linked to 43% higher risk of early death; observational caveat); Crum, Salovey & Achor 2013 stress-is-enhancing videos; Jamieson et al. 2010 reappraisal and GRE maths scores; Brooks 2014 'I am excited'; mixed replications caveat

b10: other people: Taylor et al. 2000 tend-and-befriend; Coan, Schaefer & Davidson 2006 hand holding and threat of shock (spouse's hand calmed the brain most, stronger in better marriages); Heinrichs et al. 2003 support and oxytocin lowered cortisol in the TSST; Jonah's colleague says 'you've got this'

b11: what helps, gently and research-based: Ulrich 1984 Science window view (tree view vs brick wall, shorter stays, fewer strong painkillers); Ramirez & Beilock 2011 Science writing about worries before an exam; Pennebaker & Beall 1986 expressive writing; slow breathing (Zaccaro et al. 2018 review); sleep and stress (Minkel et al. 2012); Jonah's talk went fine; takeaways; if stress feels overwhelming, talk to a doctor; turn to wind-down
b12: wind-down 1: the evening after a stressful day; the alarm can switch off now; noticing the room, the warmth, the weight of the body
b13: wind-down 2: slow breathing with longer out-breaths, counting gently; the calming branch of the nervous system (parasympathetic) in plain words, no numbers
b14: wind-down 3: putting the day's worries on a shelf / writing them down in the mind; nothing needs solving tonight
b15: wind-down 4: body scan from the forehead and jaw to the shoulders, hands, belly, legs, feet; letting tension go
b16: wind-down 5: imagined slow walk under trees to a quiet window view (callback to Ulrich), rain, soft light
b17: wind-down 6: last gentle callbacks to Jonah asleep, thank you, @end teasing Why Happiness Never Stays
